common_name: Miss Jessup Rosemary (Tall Upright Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Miss Jessup grows tall and upright, making it well suited to hedging or as a vertical accent, and tolerates the humidity of Gulf Coast summers reasonably well given sharp drainage.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, average to lean soil in full sun; rosemary is highly intolerant of wet feet, so raised beds or slightly sloped sites help in areas with heavy clay or high rainfall. Miss Jessup is a long-cultivated rosemary selection known for its tall, strongly upright growth habit, reaching four to six feet with age, which makes it one of the best rosemary cultivars for training into a low hedge, topiary, or vertical accent plant, distinct from the many low, spreading, or mounding rosemary types more commonly sold for groundcover use. The narrow, aromatic, needle-like leaves are fully useful in the kitchen, and the pale blue flowers in late winter to spring draw early-season pollinators. Prune regularly to maintain shape and encourage bushy new growth, and avoid overhead watering, since rosemary performs best on the dry side once established.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in full sun, sharply drained, lean soil; like other creeping thymes it needs excellent drainage and struggles in heavy, wet, or humid conditions.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since this low, mat-forming thyme is intolerant of wet or heavy soil and thrives on genuine neglect once established. Coconut Thyme is grown primarily as an ornamental ground cover for its dense, glossy, dark green foliage and — true to its name — a distinctly sweet, coconut-like fragrance released when leaves are brushed or crushed, an unusual scent profile among thymes that are more typically savory or lemony. Small pink flowers appear in early summer and are attractive to bees, and the tight, trailing mat is well suited to cascading over rock walls, edging pathways, or filling gaps between pavers. Avoid overhead watering and rich, moisture-retentive soil, both of which encourage root and crown rot in this drought-adapted plant.
